Proto-Germanic *īsą Proto-West Germanic *īs Old English īs Middle English is English ice From Middle English hyse, hyys, ice, ijs, is, yce, ys, yys, from Old English īs, from Proto-West Germanic *īs, from Proto-Germanic *īsą (“ice”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eyH- (“ice, frost”).

ex: He said, “Where we’re at right now was back in 2008 all covered with ice. From here to there at the side, the glacier shrank about 20 to 30 meters.”

senses.d: Any frozen volatile chemical, such as ammonia or carbon dioxide.
Any volatile chemical, such as water, ammonia, or carbon dioxide, not necessarily in solid form, when discussing the composition of e.g. a planet as an ice giant vs a gas giant.
Something having an extreme coldness of manner.
ex: Her eyes flash with anger, her voice ice. "You afraid of the law? You haven't changed. I want you out of my house now."

senses.d: Something, such as awkwardness, that prevents open social interaction.
The area where a game of ice hockey is played.
Icing; frosting ("a sweet, often creamy and thick glaze made primarily of sugar").

ex: The peach melba, probably the most famous sundae of all, is a sound marriage of poached peaches, vanilla ice and raspberry sauce.

senses.d: A frozen dessert made of fruit juice, water and sugar.
To cool with ice, as an injured body part or a beverage.

ex: The bridge ices before the road.

senses.d: To cover with icing (frosting made of sugar and milk or white of egg); to frost; as cakes, tarts, etc.
To put out a team for a match.
ex: Milton Keynes have yet to ice a team this season

senses.d: To shoot the puck the length of the playing surface, causing a stoppage in play called icing.
ex: If the Bruins ice the puck, the faceoff will be in their own zone.
Not long afterwards Wolf rings him up. 'I want you to ice someone for £15,000, he says. "No one you know."
Despite his vulnerabilities, Clinton managed to ice Dole in his 1996 reelection campaign for President.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French glace, from Old French glace (“ice", also "glass, mirror, radiance”), from Vulgar Latin *glacium/a, from Latin glaciēs (“ice”). The senses of "glass, mirror, radiance" were possibly derived from Frankish *glas (“glass”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *glacium/a, from Latin glaciēs. Doublet of ghiaccia. Compare Sicilian chiatru.
From earlier yelo, from Latin gelū, from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”). Compare English gel.
From Old Galician-Portuguese gelo, borrowed from Latin gelū, from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”). Displaced the inherited Old Portuguese geo.
Calque of English dry ice.
From Middle French nege, naige (14th c.), deverbal from neiger (“to snow”). Displaced related Old French noif, from Latin nix, nivem.

From Latin gelātus, derived from gelū (“frost, chill”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”). By surface analysis, gelo (“frost, cold”) + -ato (past participle suffix). Literally, “frozen.” Akin to Russian моро́женое (moróženoje).

Inherited from Latin gelātus, perfect passive participle of Latin gelō (“to freeze”). Cognate to Italian gelato. By surface analysis, helar (“to freeze, to cool”) + -ado (past participle suffix). Literally, “frozen.”
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin gelātus (“frozen”), from gelō (“to freeze”), from gelu (“frost”). Doublet of geado.
